params.question: In the two-axis classification of poisons described in this video, which approach directly guides a clinician in selecting the appropriate treatment?

answers.text: Classification by origin — animal, vegetable, mineral, and synthetic

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Classification by origin guides the forensic science laboratory in selecting the appropriate analytical method, not the clinician in choosing treatment.

answers.text: Classification by chemical structure — organic and inorganic compounds

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Chemical structure classification is not one of the two axes described in this framework. The two axes are classification by origin (for the forensic lab) and by action (for the clinician).

answers.text: Classification by action — corrosive, irritant, neurotic, cardiac, and asphyxiant

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The narration explains that classification by action groups poisons by their mechanism of harm, which directly tells the clinician which antidote and treatment to reach for.

answers.text: Classification by lethal dose — ranking poisons from most to least toxic

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Lethal dose ranking is not one of the two classification axes described. The framework uses origin (guiding analytical methods) and action (guiding treatment decisions).

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the two-axis framework: classification by origin helps the forensic lab choose analytical methods, while classification by action — corrosive, irritant, neurotic, cardiac, asphyxiant — helps the clinician choose the right treatment.

Well done! Classification by action groups poisons by their mechanism of harm — corrosive, irritant, neurotic, cardiac, or asphyxiant — directly guiding the clinician to the appropriate antidote and treatment strategy.

interactions.label: A patient has a chemical burn on the forearm from concentrated hydrochloric acid

params.question: A patient has a chemical burn on the forearm from concentrated hydrochloric acid. A colleague suggests applying sodium bicarbonate to neutralise the acid. What is the correct response?

answers.text: Apply sodium bicarbonate immediately — neutralisation halts the chemical injury faster than irrigation alone

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Neutralisation of acid with alkali on living tissue produces an exothermic reaction, generating heat that inflicts an additional thermal burn on top of the existing chemical injury.

answers.text: Do not neutralise — the exothermic reaction will add a thermal burn on top of the chemical injury

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The narration warns: never neutralise an acid burn with an alkali or vice versa. The resulting reaction generates heat, adding a thermal burn. Irrigate with copious water for 15–20 minutes instead.

answers.text: Neutralisation is safe only if performed within the first two minutes of exposure

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Timing does not make neutralisation safe. The exothermic reaction occurs regardless of when the neutralising agent is applied to living tissue.

answers.text: Apply sodium bicarbonate only after completing fifteen minutes of water irrigation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Sodium bicarbonate should not be applied at any stage. The correct decontamination approach is prolonged water irrigation for at least 15–20 minutes, followed by assessment for tissue damage.

overallFeedback.feedback: Never apply a neutralising agent to a chemical burn. The acid-alkali reaction generates heat, adding a thermal burn to the existing chemical injury. Irrigate with copious water for at least 15–20 minutes instead.

Correct! Neutralising an acid with an alkali on living tissue produces an exothermic reaction that causes an additional thermal burn. The correct approach is copious water irrigation for at least 15–20 minutes.

interactions.label: An unconscious patient is brought from a closed room where a charcoal fire was b

params.question: An unconscious patient is brought from a closed room where a charcoal fire was burning. The pulse oximeter shows SpO₂ of 98%. What should the treating physician conclude?

answers.text: An SpO₂ of 98% reliably excludes significant hypoxia in this patient

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Standard pulse oximetry cannot distinguish between oxyhaemoglobin and carboxyhaemoglobin, so it gives a falsely normal reading in carbon monoxide poisoning.

answers.text: The elevated SpO₂ confirms adequate ventilation despite the patient's unconsciousness

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: In CO poisoning, SpO₂ is misleadingly normal because the oximeter detects carboxyhaemoglobin as though it were oxyhaemoglobin. A normal SpO₂ does not confirm adequate oxygenation.

answers.text: Pulse oximetry is unreliable only in cyanide poisoning, not in carbon monoxide exposure

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The video specifically identifies carbon monoxide as a poison where pulse oximetry gives falsely normal readings. This is one of the most important bedside test limitations in clinical toxicology.

answers.text: The reading is falsely reassuring — pulse oximetry cannot distinguish carboxyhaemoglobin from oxyhaemoglobin, and co-oximetry is needed

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Pulse oximetry reads falsely normal in CO poisoning because it cannot differentiate carboxyhaemoglobin from oxyhaemoglobin. Co-oximetry, which measures multiple haemoglobin species, is essential here.

overallFeedback.feedback: In carbon monoxide poisoning, standard pulse oximetry gives a falsely normal SpO₂ because carboxyhaemoglobin absorbs light similarly to oxyhaemoglobin. Co-oximetry is essential to detect CO poisoning.
Well done! Pulse oximetry cannot differentiate carboxyhaemoglobin from oxyhaemoglobin, making it unreliable in CO poisoning. Always request co-oximetry when carbon monoxide exposure is suspected.

interactions.label: At medico-legal autopsy, white, soapy-looking tissue damage around the mouth is

params.question: At medico-legal autopsy, white, soapy-looking tissue damage around the mouth is characteristic of poisoning by a strong acid.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This statement is false. The narration states that acids leave grey or black tissue damage, while alkalis leave white, soapy-looking burns. Confusing the two can mislead the forensic investigation and delay identification of the causative substance.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — this statement is false. White, soapy-looking burns are caused by strong alkalis through liquefactive necrosis. Strong acids produce grey or black tissue damage through coagulative necrosis. Distinguishing these patterns helps narrow the substance class before laboratory confirmation.

interactions.label: The video describes methylmercury in water and DDT in soil as persistent environ

params.question: The video describes methylmercury in water and DDT in soil as persistent environmental toxins. What common property makes both substances particularly dangerous to humans at the top of the food chain?

answers.text: Both bioaccumulate and biomagnify up the food chain, reaching highest concentrations in top predators including humans

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The narration emphasises that both methylmercury and DDT share bioaccumulation and biomagnification — each trophic level concentrates the toxin further, so humans as top predators receive the highest doses.

answers.text: Both are highly volatile, causing direct inhalation toxicity across large geographic areas

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Neither methylmercury nor DDT is primarily dangerous through volatility or inhalation. Their danger lies in progressive accumulation through the food chain, not atmospheric exposure.

answers.text: Both bind irreversibly to haemoglobin, causing chronic hypoxia even at very low concentrations

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Irreversible haemoglobin binding is the mechanism of carbon monoxide toxicity, not methylmercury or DDT. These environmental toxins act through entirely different pathways.

answers.text: Both are water-soluble heavy metals that accumulate in the renal tubules over time

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: DDT is an organochlorine pesticide, not a heavy metal. Its lipophilicity — not water solubility — enables biomagnification in the fat stores of organisms up the food chain.

overallFeedback.feedback: The common thread is bioaccumulation and biomagnification. Both methylmercury and DDT persist in the environment and concentrate in organisms at each trophic level, reaching dangerous levels in top predators including humans.

Correct! The narration highlights the common thread: both methylmercury and DDT persist in the environment and concentrate at each step of the food chain, making top predators including humans the most heavily exposed.
